strengths: The core idea — combining off-the-shelf sparse, dense, and neural retrievers in a training-free cascade for open-domain table QA — is practical and relevant, and the paper convincingly shows that careful pipeline design can rival fine-tuned retrievers without in-domain training.

The ablation studies are unusually thorough: stage-by-stage contributions (Tables 5, 6, 8, 9, 10), effects of table descriptions, query decomposition, few-shot prompting (Table 12), sub-table vs. full-table token costs (Table 13), and retrieval-depth sweeps are all reported.

The robustness analysis under LLM-generated query paraphrasing (Table 2) is a nice addition, showing the training-free cascade degrades far less than fine-tuned DTR models, addressing a real weakness of specialized retrievers.
Prompts used for answer generation, table description, and query expansion are provided, and model configurations are documented, partially supporting reproducibility.
The end-to-end evaluation spans multiple LLMs (Mistral, Llama3, Qwen2.5, plus larger instruct models) and multiple retrieval depths, giving a reasonably broad empirical picture.
weaknesses: Overclaiming and internal contradictions undermine confidence in the central claims: the abstract states CRAFT achieves 'better retrieval performance than SOTA,' yet Table 1 shows THYME wins at R@1 (48.55 vs. 41.13) and the text itself concedes THYME has the best average performance. Similarly, the text claims Mistral-Small-Instruct at F1 50.26 'already surpasses' LI-RAGE at 54.17, which is numerically false, and claims CRAFT 'consistently outperforms' baselines when Table 3 shows losses (e.g., Qwen n=1: 33.33 vs. THYME 37.28).

The evaluation is confined to a single benchmark (NQ-Tables), which the authors acknowledge; the generalizability of the pipeline to other TQA datasets or genuinely 'in-the-wild' settings remains untested despite claims about TQA-in-the-wild superiority.

Comparisons are not strictly apples-to-apples: baselines were reportedly trained on NQ-Tables and some are scored on the full 966-query test set (per the '*' note) while CRAFT uses 919 unique queries; the paper does not clarify whether all numbers are directly comparable. No statistical significance testing or variance estimates are provided for any comparison.

The 'training-free' framing is somewhat misleading: the pipeline depends on Gemini-1.5-Flash to generate titles, descriptions, and sub-questions for the entire 169,898-table corpus, which is a nontrivial, dataset-specific preprocessing step with API cost. There is also an unaddressed risk of leakage, since generated descriptions could implicitly encode question/answer-like information from NQ-derived content.

Reproducibility is limited by reliance on closed, versioned API models (Gemini, OpenAI text-embedding-3-small) whose behavior may change; no code or generated artifacts are stated as released, and inference latency of the three-stage cascade is never measured despite scalability and efficiency claims.

Novelty is modest: cascaded (sparse → dense → rerank) retrieval is a well-established pattern, and the components are standard off-the-shelf models; the contribution is largely an engineering configuration rather than a new method or insight.

The paper contains multiple writing and consistency errors that suggest insufficient polish: 'prepossessing,' contradictory stage-flow descriptions in Appendix A.1, a 'DPR version trained with hard negatives' that presumably means DTR (Table 2 discussion), THYME cited with two different author sets (Li et al. 2025 vs. Zhao et al. 2024), and a misplaced baseline training-configuration table (Table 11) in the appendix with no explanation of how baselines were re-run.

The robustness gains, while directionally interesting, are modest (CRAFT Δ ≈ -0.04 average) and the perturbation generator (Gemini 2.5 Flash) is not validated, leaving the quality/difficulty of perturbed queries unknown.

strengths: The paper targets a relevant problem (open-domain tabular QA retrieval) and the proposed training-free cascaded pipeline is a reasonable and practical design that combines sparse filtering, semantic refinement, and neural reranking with off-the-shelf models.

The ablation studies (stage-wise results, effect of table descriptions, query decomposition, and sub-table vs. full-table token analysis in the appendix) are relatively thorough and give useful engineering insight.

The robustness experiment under perturbed queries is an interesting angle, and the observation that the cascade largely recovers performance under paraphrasing (where fine-tuned DTR models degrade substantially) is a potentially valuable finding.
The end-to-end evaluation across multiple LLMs and retrieval depths (n=1,3,5,8,10) with both zero-shot and few-shot prompting provides breadth.
weaknesses: Overclaiming relative to the evidence: the abstract claims CRAFT 'achieves better retrieval performance than SOTA sparse, dense, and hybrid retrievers,' yet Table 1 shows THYME achieves substantially higher R@1 (48.55 vs. 41.13) and the paper itself concedes THYME has the best average performance. CRAFT only wins marginally at R@10 and R@50.

A glaring internal contradiction in the end-to-end analysis: the text claims Mistral-Small-Instruct 'achieves an F1 score of 50.26, already surpassing the best-performing baseline, LI-RAGE (54.17)' — 50.26 does not surpass 54.17. This kind of unsupported claim severely undermines confidence in the analysis.

Unfair/unclear comparison protocol: CRAFT is evaluated on 919 unique queries while several baselines (e.g., T-RAG, THYME) are reported on the full 966-query test set; this mismatch is flagged in a footnote but never resolved or justified, and it is unclear whether Table 1/3 baseline numbers were reproduced or copied from prior work. Table 11 ('Training and inference configuration used for all baselines') is confusing given the paper's training-free premise.

The end-to-end claim that CRAFT 'consistently outperforms' baselines is contradicted by Table 3, where CRAFT with Qwen at n=1 (33.33) loses to BIBERT (34.80), and several other settings show mixed results. No statistical significance testing or variance reporting is provided anywhere.

The paper relies on proprietary, closed models (Gemini-1.5-Flash for corpus-scale preprocessing of 169,898 tables and query decomposition, Gemini 2.5 Flash for perturbations, OpenAI text-embedding-3-small for reranking), raising serious reproducibility and cost concerns; no code or generated artifacts are stated to be released, and no cost/latency analysis of the full pipeline is given.

Limited novelty: cascaded retrieval (sparse first-stage filtering followed by dense reranking) is standard IR practice, and the main new ingredients (LLM-generated table descriptions/titles and query decomposition) are well-known techniques; the contribution is largely an engineering application to NQ-Tables.

Evaluation is confined to a single benchmark (NQ-Tables), which the limitations section acknowledges, and the R@1 deficit versus THYME is hand-waved with an unverified claim that other tables also contain the answer, with no supporting analysis.

Sign inconsistencies and sloppy writing further reduce clarity: Table 2 reports a positive Δ for CRAFT Stage 1 under perturbation while the text says Stage 1 'drops performance by 3.4%'; the text also refers to 'DPR version trained with hard negatives' where DTR is meant; the pipeline description contains redundancies (e.g., 'These 5,000 re-ranked tables then serve as the input to Stage 1').

strengths: The cascaded retrieval idea (sparse filtering with SPLADE → dense re-ranking with a sentence transformer → neural re-ranking with a stronger embedder) is sensible, well-motivated, and modular; the paper presents a clear pipeline description with prompts and hyperparameters included in the appendix.

Comprehensive ablation studies: stage-wise recall gains, effect of LLM-generated table descriptions, effect of query decomposition, sub-table vs. full-table token costs, and variation over the number of retrieved tables and few-shot examples give a fairly complete picture of design choices.

The robustness analysis under LLM-generated query paraphrases is an interesting angle, and the finding that the training-free cascade degrades far less than fine-tuned DTR models (-0.04 vs. -5.8 to -11.82 average recall) is a genuinely valuable result.

Evaluating end-to-end TQA with multiple LLMs (Mistral, Llama3, Qwen2.5) and multiple context sizes adds practical relevance, and the topic of training-free open-domain table QA is relevant to the community.
A limitations section is present and appropriately identifies the single-benchmark scope and inference-cost trade-off.
weaknesses: Overclaiming relative to the evidence: the abstract claims 'better retrieval performance than SOTA' retrievers, but Table 1 shows THYME substantially outperforms CRAFT at R@1 (48.55 vs. 41.13); CRAFT only wins at R@10/R@50. Similarly, the text claims Mistral-Small-Instruct at n=1 (F1 50.26) 'already surpasses' LI-RAGE (54.17), which is numerically false. The claim that few-shot prompting 'enhances performance substantially across all models' is contradicted by Table 3/12, where 5-shot Llama3 drops from 44.06 to 39.39 at n=3 and several few-shot variants underperform zero-shot.

Internal inconsistencies undermine confidence: Table 2 shows Stage 2 degrading more under paraphrase (Δ=-6.5) than Stage 1 (Δ=-3.41), yet the text claims 'Stage 2 partly recovers it'; the text refers to a 'DPR version trained with hard negatives' when DTR is meant; Table 1's footnote convention for query counts (919 vs. 966) makes cross-method comparability unclear — it is never stated whether CRAFT and the trained baselines are evaluated on the same query set.

Reliance on closed-source commercial APIs (Gemini-1.5-Flash for generating titles/descriptions/sub-queries for all ~170k tables, text-embedding-3-small for re-ranking) with no code or data release mentioned severely limits reproducibility; the 'training-free' framing also obscures a corpus-specific LLM preprocessing pass whose cost is never quantified.

Evaluation on a single benchmark (NQ-Tables) limits generalization claims; NQ-Tables is a somewhat saturated benchmark where the training-free vs. fine-tuned comparison is also confounded — the LLM-enriched descriptions effectively inject additional knowledge, so 'no training' does not mean 'no dataset adaptation'.

No efficiency analysis of the cascade itself: the paper's core motivation is computational cost, yet there are no latency/indexing-cost measurements for the three-stage pipeline versus a single strong retriever, and the trade-off discussion is qualitative only.
No statistical significance testing or variance estimates for the LLM-based end-to-end results, which the appendix itself admits exhibit high variability with few-shot prompting.

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation: the paper covers two standard benchmarks (NQ-Tables, OTT-QA), compares against sparse, dense, and hybrid retrievers including recent SOTA (THYME, LI-RAGE, SSDR), and evaluates end-to-end QA across multiple open and closed LLMs.

Thorough ablation studies that isolate each component's contribution: table descriptions (Table 9), query decomposition (Table 10), row filtering/mini-tables (Table 11), and reranking depth (Table 12), showing each stage contributes measurable recall gains.

A novel and useful robustness analysis under LLM-generated query paraphrasing (Table 4), demonstrating that the cascade nearly fully recovers performance while fine-tuned DTR baselines degrade substantially.

Careful computational-efficiency analysis: explicit accounting of online embedding calls, token-count reductions from mini-tables (70%+ reduction, Table 7), and latency/cost trade-offs, which is rare and valuable for a systems-oriented paper.

Qualitative error analysis with concrete case studies (Tables 16-17) that meaningfully illustrate why mini-table representations help downstream QA, including the interesting finding that R@1 underestimates end-to-end capability.
Clearly stated limitations section, and full prompts for LLM-based components provided in the appendix, which supports some degree of reproducibility.
weaknesses: The 'training-free / zero-shot' framing is overstated. The pipeline depends heavily on offline Gemini-1.5-Flash generation of table titles, descriptions, and sub-questions for the entire corpus (169K-419K tables). This is a significant, undisclosed-cost LLM preprocessing step, and the paper does not report its cost or quantify its contribution separately from other stages in a way that fully justifies the framing.

Comparison fairness is questionable. CRAFT combines very large closed-source models (text-embedding-3-large, gemini-embedding-001, GPT-4o) against fine-tuned academic-scale baselines, while claiming credit for beating 'expensive domain-specialized' methods. Additionally, the paper is inconsistent about which SPLADE variant is used (supervised vs. base), which muddies the Stage 1 baseline comparison.

Reproducibility concerns: the stated code/data link is missing/dangling in the submission; core components rely on closed, versioned commercial APIs (Gemini, OpenAI embeddings, GPT-4o) whose behavior may change; no statistical significance testing or variance reporting despite noting 'greater performance variability' in few-shot settings.

Internal inconsistencies in the results: Table 4 reports CRAFT R@50 = 96.84 (small embedding model) while Table 2 reports 97.17 for full CRAFT (large model), and Table 8's CRAFT row has missing entries; the hyperparameter appendix (Table 13) describes training configurations (epochs, learning rate) that appear to belong to baselines but are ambiguously presented, and 50 training epochs for baselines raises questions about whether baselines were tuned comparably.

Novelty is moderate: cascaded first-stage-sparse/late-stage-dense retrieval, LLM-generated document expansion, and query decomposition are all established techniques (Wang et al. 2011, Re2G, doc2query-style expansion); the contribution is primarily a careful engineering integration and empirical study rather than a new method.

OTT-QA end-to-end evaluation is only in an oracle setting (gold passages paired with retrieved tables), so the strong 'zero-shot on OTT-QA' claim in the abstract is not supported by a fully open-retrieval end-to-end result.

Writing and presentation issues: several grammatical errors, a dense Figure 1, dense/overlapping line plots in Figures 2, 6, 7, and some imprecise claims (e.g., '33x fewer online embedding calls' that should be contextualized against the 5,100 per-query mini-table embeddings, which is itself a large per-query cost).

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and practical question: whether carefully composed off-the-shelf retrieval components can match fine-tuned table retrievers, which is of interest to the CL/NLP community.
The evaluation covers two standard benchmarks (NQ-Tables, OTT-QA) with multiple baselines across sparse, dense, and hybrid categories, and reports results at several recall depths.
End-to-end QA experiments with multiple LLMs (Mistral, Llama3, Qwen, GPT-4o) and varying retrieval depths provide a reasonably broad picture of downstream utility.

The ablation studies (Stage 1 description/query-expansion effects, Stage 2 row filtering, Stage 3 reranking depth) and the token-footprint analysis (Tables 7, 9-12) are a useful attempt to attribute gains to individual components.
A limitations section exists and honestly flags the oracle setting for OTT-QA end-to-end evaluation and the single-hop scope.
weaknesses: Unfair and incomparable baseline setting: CRAFT relies on large, modern commercial embedding models (text-embedding-3-large, gemini-embedding-001) and offline Gemini-1.5-Flash generation of titles/descriptions for ~170K-420K tables, while most baselines are older fine-tuned models. The decisive ablation — embedding all tables with text-embedding-3-large directly (no cascade) and comparing — is missing, so it is unclear whether the cascade or simply the stronger embedder drives the claimed SOTA. The 'training-free' framing obscures substantial offline LLM precomputation whose cost is never quantified.

The claimed SOTA on NQ-Tables is fragile: with text-embedding-3-small, Stage 3 gives R@1 41.13 vs THYME's 48.55; only the large embedder (49.84) surpasses it, and R@10 is essentially tied (86.83 vs 86.72). No significance testing or variance estimates are reported anywhere.

Internal inconsistencies in reported numbers: OTT-QA Stage 2 R@10 is 81.88 in Table 3 but 87.35 in Table 8; R@50 appears as 91.82 (Table 3) vs 96.07 (Table 8) for overlapping configurations. These discrepancies undermine confidence in the experimental bookkeeping.

A misleading claim in Section 4.2: 'With the original queries, CRAFT already outperforms the DTR baselines' — Table 4 shows CRAFT at 41.13 R@1 versus DTR(M)+HN at 47.33, so CRAFT is actually worse on R@1 for original queries; the robustness argument is built on a partially incorrect premise.

OTT-QA end-to-end evaluation uses an oracle setting (gold passages), admitted only in the Limitations; the abstract's claim of 'strong zero-shot performance' on OTT-QA is therefore weaker than presented, and CRAFT still trails fine-tuned hybrids on R@1.

Reproducibility is not delivered: the abstract ends with 'Code and data are available at:' with no URL, and the pipeline depends on proprietary, versioned APIs (Gemini 1.5/2.5 Flash, OpenAI embeddings, gemini-embedding-001) whose outputs cannot be regenerated reliably; prompts are provided but no seeds, prompts for DTR comparison, or variance details.

Novelty is limited: cascaded retrieve-then-rerank pipelines, query expansion, and LLM-generated table descriptions are established techniques; the mini-table (top-5 rows) representation is the main design element and its contribution is plausible but modest.

Presentation issues reduce clarity: Section 3.1's 'Firstly... Finally' preprocessing description omits a middle step and mixes preprocessing with per-query operations; Table 8 is cluttered with boxed-value conventions that are hard to parse; Appendix Table 13 describes training hyperparameters 'used for all baselines' without explaining whether baselines were retrained by the authors or taken from prior work, which affects comparability.

The efficiency claims (33x fewer embedding calls, 70% shorter contexts) are stated without end-to-end latency or monetary cost measurements, and Stage 2's on-the-fly mini-table embedding of 5,000 tables per query is acknowledged to raise per-query latency but never quantified against the dense baseline.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically relevant question for computational linguistics and NLP: whether training-free, plug-and-play retrieval pipelines over tables can compete with fine-tuned, dataset-specialized retrievers (DTR, THYME, LI-RAGE, etc.). The framing is clear and the experimental question is well motivated.

The evaluation is broad and reasonably rigorous: two standard benchmarks (NQ-Tables, OTT-QA), comparisons against sparse, dense, and hybrid baselines, stage-wise ablations (Tables 8-12), a query-paraphrasing robustness study (Table 4), end-to-end QA with multiple LLMs and retrieval depths (Tables 5, 6, 14), and token-cost analyses (Table 7, Figure 2).

The mini-table representation is a genuinely useful engineering contribution, supported by both quantitative evidence (70%+ token reduction, +R@10 from row filtering in Table 11) and qualitative case studies (Tables 16-17) showing that full-table context causes hallucination even when the gold table is retrieved.

The robustness analysis under LLM-generated query paraphrasing is a nice addition that goes beyond standard recall benchmarks and directly supports the claim that the cascade recovers performance lost by a fine-tuned dense retriever (DTR).
The paper is largely transparent about limitations, including the oracle setting for OTT-QA end-to-end evaluation and per-query latency increases.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is weakened by heavy dependence on closed-source, commercial APIs (Gemini 1.5 Flash for all table titles/descriptions and query expansions over 169K-419K tables, text-embedding-3-small/large, gemini-embedding-001, GPT-4o). Model versions may be deprecated, and the offline LLM preprocessing cost (API calls over the full corpus) is never quantified, which undercuts the 'training-free / efficient' framing: the pipeline shifts cost from fine-tuning to expensive offline LLM annotation.
The abstract promises 'Code and data are available at:' but no actual URL is given in the provided manuscript, a concrete reproducibility gap.

Claimed SOTA on NQ-Tables rests on thin margins (R@1 49.84 vs. THYME 48.55) with no statistical significance testing or variance estimates, and on R@10 CRAFT with the large embedder (86.83) actually trails its own small-embedder variant (87.16) and other results are mixed, so 'outperforms SOTA' is overstated in places.

Fairness of comparisons is questionable in the end-to-end setting: CRAFT paired with GPT-4o is compared against baselines (RAG, DPR-RAGE, LI-RAGE) built on far weaker generators, so F1 gains conflate retrieval quality with generator strength; a same-LLM controlled comparison across retrievers exists only for the 7-8B models (Table 5).

Internal inconsistencies and unclear reporting: Stage 2 shows a larger perturbation drop than Stage 1 (Δ -6.5 vs -3.41) yet the text claims 'Stage 2 partly recovers it'; Table 8's boxed-value convention is confusing; Table 13 (hyperparameters including THYME dropout and training epochs) sits oddly in an otherwise 'training-free' paper and its purpose for baselines is under-explained.

Novelty is moderate: cascaded retrieve-then-rerank pipelines, LLM-based document/query expansion, and mini-table row filtering are each established ideas; the contribution is primarily a well-executed system combination rather than a new method, which limits main-conference-level impact.

OTT-QA end-to-end results are only in an oracle setting with gold passages, so the multi-hop claims remain untested in a realistic pipeline; the OTT-QA retrieval gaps to fine-tuned baselines at R@1 (55.56 vs 66.67) are substantial and glossed over in favor of high-depth recall comparisons.

Writing quality issues (typos such as 'a differnt', inconsistent notation like N3 defined as 'number of tables in the corpus' when it means number of reranked tables) and some hand-wavy prose (e.g., 'preventing noise amplification') reduce clarity.
